Company: CornerCare Pharmacy

US drugstore chain with 300 neighborhood pharmacies in the Midwest (~6,000 employees). Fills prescriptions (including controlled painkillers and ADHD medicines), gives flu and COVID shots, and sells over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, snacks and household goods. Most prescriptions are paid by Medicare, Medicaid or private insurance. No hospitals or clinics, does not make any drugs, no mail-order.

Rules that APPLY:
- DEA rules for pharmacies that dispense controlled substances (registration, opioids, telehealth prescribing)
- FDA rules on over-the-counter drugs, drug labeling, drug shortages and recalls that reach pharmacy shelves
- Medicare Part D and Medicaid payment and pharmacy rules (CMS)
- CDC vaccine recommendations that change what pharmacists may give
- Patient privacy (HIPAA) and pharmacy recordkeeping
- Workplace and labor rules for retail stores

Rules that DO NOT apply:
- Approval, manufacturing or inspection rules aimed only at drug or device manufacturers
- Hospital, nursing-home, physician-payment or clinical-lab rules
- Research grants, clinical trials, NIH funding notices
- Banking, securities, aviation, energy, farming

[2026-22203] Notice — Health and Human Services Department; Food and Drug Administration

Action: Notice of availability.
Abstract: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is announcing the availability of a revised draft guidance for industry entitled "Essential Drug Delivery Performance Characteristics for Devices Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products." This revised draft guidance revises and replaces the draft guidance entitled "Essential Drug Delivery Outputs Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products" announced in the Federal Register on July 1, 2024 (89 FR 54470). In accordance with its mission of protecting, promoting, and advancing public health, this guidance addresses key aspects of drug delivery performance information for devices, and combination products that include device constituent parts, intended for delivery of a human drug, including a biological product (herein referred to as drug delivery devices). This guidance provides recommendations for development and organization of device drug-delivery performance information and data to improve the consistency of this information in applications and to facilitate transparency and predictability in development and regulatory review. [2026-21821] Rule — Federal Communications Commission
Title: Enhancing the Ability of Consumers To Control the Robocalls
Action: Final rule.
Abstract: In this document, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) modifies rules to ensure that consumers can revoke consent for robocalls they no longer wish to receive while continuing to receive those they still want. We also modernize our rules to ensure that consumers have clear, simple, and automated ways to revoke consent while streamlining callers' ability to process revocations. Specifically, we allow callers to interpret a revocation request as applying only to the specific category of informational robocalls to which the revocation was directed, allow callers to designate an exclusive means to revoke consent, and amend the exemption from the consent requirement for financial institutions to allow them to more easily alert customers to fraudulent activity on their account. In addition, we delegate authority to the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau (CGB) in consultation with the Enforcement Bureau (EB) to review our robocall rules to ensure that those rules are clear and easy to read.

# Regulatory triage — CornerCare Pharmacy
Window 2026-10-26 → 2026-10-30 · as of 2026-10-30 · 2 items

## Critical (2)

- **Schedules of Controlled Substances: Placement of Centanafadine in Schedule III** [Federal Register]
  - Direct pharmacies to treat centanafadine, the new ADHD drug, as a Schedule III controlled substance, updating storage, recordkeeping, prescription and refill procedures to stay compliant.
  - Dates: effective 2026-10-30 ✓ · comment 2026-11-30 ✓ · other 2026-11-30 ✓ · Owner: Priya Raman (Pharmacy Operations) · Areas: pharmacy-ops
  - 91 FR 68470 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/30/2026-22208/schedules-of-controlled-substances-placement-of-centanafadine-in-schedule-iii
- **Enhancing the Ability of Consumers To Control the Robocalls** [Federal Register]
  - Update automated refill and vaccine reminder calls and texts so patient requests to stop messages are honored promptly, avoiding costly consumer-protection violations and lawsuits.
  - Dates: effective 2026-11-25 ✓ · Owner: Sam Whitaker (Privacy & HR Compliance) · Areas: privacy-people
  - 91 FR 67214 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/26/2026-21821/enhancing-the-ability-of-consumers-to-control-the-robocalls

votes.why: Plain-English instruction to pharmacies to handle centanafadine as Schedule III, with concrete procedures to update.
Matches the reason (Schedule III, ADHD drug, storage/records/prescription/refill controls) and avoids claiming Schedule II or a merely proposed status.
States that centanafadine, an ADHD drug, is Schedule III and that pharmacies must apply controlled-substance procedures.
A non-lawyer can follow it: update reminder calls and texts so stop requests are honored promptly.
Consistent with the reason about honoring consent revocations for refill and vaccine reminders; the lawsuit-risk framing is a reasonable general consequence, not a specific unsupported claim.
It gives the owner one concrete next step: direct pharmacies to update how they handle centanafadine.
The Schedule III classification and listed pharmacy controls are supported, and the action makes neither prohibited claim.
It identifies centanafadine as a Schedule III ADHD drug and tells pharmacies to apply the corresponding controlled-substance procedures.
It gives the owner one concrete next step in plain English: update automated reminders so patients' stop requests are honored promptly.
The reason supports updating how stop requests are handled, but it does not establish that the update will avoid costly violations or lawsuits.
The action is written in plain English and gives Pharmacy Operations one concrete step to update Schedule III handling procedures for centanafadine.
The action stays faithful to the Schedule III controls described in the reason and avoids all prohibited claims in the rubric.
It conveys both that centanafadine is an ADHD drug placed in Schedule III and that pharmacies must apply controlled-substance handling rules to it.
The action uses plain, non-legal language to direct a single concrete update to automated patient call and text workflows.
Neither the title nor the reason supports the specific claim that the rule change is about honoring revocations 'promptly' or involves lawsuits.
